terms.prefLabel: Report the verdict on the tracking issue
terms.definition: Runs the shared tracking watch with the label `ci-health`. Asked of the same `verdict`, once it is known. `clean` is verdict == 'clean' (exit 0): the open `ci-health` issue, if there is one, is closed saying main is clean. `not clean` is verdict == 'red' (exit 1 with a report): the one open issue labelled `ci-health` is edited in place with the report as its body, or created if there is none. Neither branch fails the job — a red main speaks through the issue, not through this workflow's status. Clean here means main is clean.

terms.prefLabel: Run check:ci-health, WRITING the report file
terms.definition: Run check:ci-health --out, writing the report file before any exit path. Exit 0 clean, 1 live failures, 2 could not check. bun also exits 1 on an uncaught exception, so an exit 1 with no report file is a crash and is treated as could-not-check. Where its verdict comes from: Asked of the `verdict` output that the `check` step of .github/workflows/ci-health.yml writes, not of the raw exit code. `check:ci-health` exits 0 clean, 1 live failure(s), 2 could not check; an exit 1 with no report file is a crash and is reclassified as could-not-check, as is any other code. `no` is verdict == 'unknown': the last step runs `exit 1` and no issue step runs, so the tracking issue is left untouched. `yes` is verdict != 'unknown', the guard on the label step and so on both issue paths.
Every finding is answered — implemented, or replied to with why not. A design question does not excuse skipping the nits in the same review.

Announce the branch WHEN IT IS CREATED, not when the work is done. The gap between one agent's view of an issue and everyone else's is what this closes.

A closed work item is read later by somebody deciding whether to reopen the subject, so "completed" with nothing behind it cannot be audited. An ISSUE is never closed on the agent's own say-so.

"Flake" is not a root cause. A red PR is work now, whatever its review state — only a green, mergeable head waits on reviewers.
The loop's only open-ended step. Everything around it is procedure; this is the work.

A human or an agent acting AS reviewer. Nothing is a reviewer; somebody acts as one for the duration of this lane. For a rendered change the reviewer reads the agent's before/after preview rather than building one. On agent-touched changes, an adversarial code review evaluates against the RED FLAG taxonomy and writes a committed verdict.

Install Chromium, check the rendered BPMN SVGs are current, then run the Playwright suite, which includes the accessibility checks. Hard: a failure blocks the PR. SHARDED since bean `dlqu` (drawn as one task, deliberately: a multi-instance marker would add a BPMN term to every instance's UML overview, about 75 generated files, for a picture this sentence already gives): the suite runs as three `e2e-shard` jobs (`E2E_SHARD=i/3`, one Playwright worker per core in each), and each shard is its own required check, so a shard that failed, was cancelled or never ran is a red check of its own. Until bean `5p4m` (issue #2456) an `e2e` job carried one check name for the three and completed the task only when every instance succeeded; it was ~1 s of work behind a runner request that waited minutes, and was removed. Measured before the split: `playwright test` alone was 4m33s of a 5m16s job, the workflow's slowest once `bun test` ran in parallel. The BPMN-render and `.bat`-wrapper checks run in shard 1 only, so they are asked once.

FOUR QUESTIONS, ONE RUNNER — bean `7fu5`. They were four jobs (`lean-bare-import`, `python-imports`, `rust-wildcard`, `dependency-advisories`), each about a second of work behind a ~13 s checkout and a runner request; measured on `main` run 37133247484 (2026-10-03), the run took 21.7 min while its longest job executed for 174 s, the rest waiting for runners. Now they are steps of the `hygiene` job, and every step after the first gate runs `if: !cancelled()`, so a red one masks none of the others — the `om30` rule kept inside one job rather than by splitting it. (1) Lean, HARD: fail on any bare `import Mathlib` in content/**/*.lean; in this platform repo there is no content/, so the step prints SKIP and states that nothing was scanned. (2) Python, HARD: ruff F401 (unused) and F403 (wildcard) over the Python trees that exist, then the Python tests; an absent tree is dropped rather than passed to ruff, and an empty set says SKIP. (3) Dependency advisories, WARN-ONLY by the owner's ruling on bean `j41m`: is anything in the resolved tree KNOWN-VULNERABLE? The script exits 0 in every state and keeps them apart in its output; `.github/dependabot.yml` is the other half of that ruling and is not drawn here. (4) Rust wildcard imports, WARN-ONLY: report non-test `use …::*;` in tools/**/*.rs; `continue-on-error`, and therefore the job's LAST step, where it masks nothing.

Bean `16ei`, arc `3fva`. After Task_RepositoryGates, WHATEVER it concluded (`needs:` its two corpus parts, with `always()`), and after Task_QaWorkingCopy, whose copy it restores and publishes rather than building a second time (bean `jtfk`), `qa:publish --github` writes this run's `test/results` trees to the orphan `qa-reports` branch: `main/<sha>/` on a push to main, `pr/<n>/<head-sha>/` on a same-repository PR (owner rulings D1, D3). A fork PR's token is read-only, so it is skipped with a `::notice` naming why. It does NOT reach GW_Join: a red publish is its own red and never decides mergeability, and the hard gates never wait on it. The only job here holding `contents: write`, which is also how `bun run cat gates` knows not to run it locally. A CALL ACTIVITY: the key derivation, the fork skip and the never-`-f` retry loop are `qa-publish.bpmn`, which also draws the retention run that takes entries off the branch again.

terms.prefLabel: QA working copy, built once (NOT A GATE)
terms.definition: Bean `jtfk`, issue #2456. `bun run qa:working-copy` (bean `72a8`) — the bootstrap kg-export, then every declared QA writer — used to run INSIDE each job that reads the QA tree, and `qa-publish` ran the same writers again: nine builds of one tree from one commit, measured at 2,284 of 4,714 runner-seconds (48 %) on run 37659324493. Now the `qa-working-copy` job builds it once and uploads everything the build changed as an artifact with a sha256 manifest; each reader downloads it, checks the manifest against the hash this job reported and every restored file against the manifest, and only then judges. An artifact rather than a cache, because a cache key built from less than the real inputs serves stale data; an artifact is per run and exact. It judges nothing, so it is not a gate and does not reach GW_Join; a failed build fails every reader at its first step (they run `if: !cancelled()`), never a skip. Drawn feeding GW_Readers, the four tasks that wait for it; within them `typescript-static` and `gates-standalone` read no QA tree and do not wait, and `qa-publish` waits for it as well as for Task_RepositoryGates.

The 43 repository-gate steps — workflow refs, lane and process documentation, kg:audit:check, detangle, skills, published packages — 150 `bun run` invocations in all. A SEPARATE job from Task_TypeScript since bean `om30`: they were one job in which `bun test` came second of 47 steps, and because Actions stops a job at its first failing step and no step was continue-on-error, a deliberate test failure on `main` meant none of these ran. A gate never asked and a gate that passed are indistinguishable from outside, which is `xom7` at the step rather than the workflow. No sequence dependency on Task_TypeScript is drawn because there is none: a red test must not stop these being asked. `bun run cat gates` derives its list from BOTH jobs, so the local set still cannot drift from CI's.

Runs the five `--check` commands that adding a skill stales, each on its own: gen-skill-docs, check:glossary, auto:docs:check, kg:audit:check, kg:detangle:check. CORRECTED 2026-09-26, after main split this workflow: the original justification is GONE. It read "the only place those five are read against the tree as checked out", because at the time all six lived in one job behind `bun test`, which runs the kg-audit and detangle WRITERS and repaired two artefacts before their checks read them (bean `ymsu`). Task_RepositoryGates is now a separate job that runs all six and never runs `bun test`, so they are unmasked THERE. What survives is narrower and is the reason this is kept: one command a skill author runs (`bun run cat skill:register`) that regenerates and verifies the chain together, a committed QA sidecar saying which steps ran, and ONE named failure instead of six unrelated generated files — which is bean `v625`'s actual complaint. The unmasking argument belongs to Task_RepositoryGates now. Its first CI run earned the place: it went red on `kg:detangle:check` and the cause was `kg-detangle.ts` counting 1214 files of a gitignored `node_modules/` as graph nodes — 1441 where a clean checkout computes 227, pinned in a committed sidecar. Not a step in front of `bun test` either: measured on main's run 36234052354, a failing step SKIPS every step behind it, so a red there would turn one named failure into forty-five unevaluated ones. 13s, in parallel. Beans `v625`, `fjwi`.

Three checks: `bun run cat lint`, `tsc --noEmit` and `bun test`. The repository gates it used to carry are Task_RepositoryGates now (bean `om30`). Since bean `dlqu` it is split across jobs: `typescript-static` (lint, then typecheck), `typescript-test` (`bun test` as four SEQUENTIAL shards on separate machines — Bun's in-process `--parallel` worker pool hung at both 4 and 2 workers, measured — the shard passed in `BUN_OPTIONS` so the command stays the one `bun run cat gates` runs locally) each shard and `typescript-static` its own required check. A fourth job, `typescript`, carried one check name for all of them and was green only when the others succeeded; bean `5p4m` (issue #2456) removed it — a runner request for ~1 s of work that waited minutes for a runner — so branch protection names the five checks directly. The step-order rule the single job needed — `bun test` LAST, because Actions stops at the first failing step and a red-by-decision test would otherwise mask lint and typecheck — no longer has anything to order: separate jobs cannot mask each other. Measured on three `main` runs before the change: `bun test` alone was 7m30s-7m45s of an 8m14s-8m33s job.

`check:gates-registered`, split out of Task_RepositoryGates by bean `dlqu`: one step of that job measured 1m46s-2m28s across four runs, the longest step in it by a factor of four, and a sequential job is as slow as the sum of its steps. In its own job it runs beside the rest rather than after them. It still asks the same question — is every gate a script registers actually run somewhere — and is still hard. It also carries `bun run cat security:gate` (bean `ieum`, owner 2026-10-07: "security check before release"): the security checks by name, plus third-party action SHA pinning outside staging-only workflows, as one step that merge-train's gate call reaches. A blocking fail OR could-not-check fails the job.

terms.prefLabel: Verdict reuse: tree already green? (NOT A GATE)
terms.definition: Bean `qbco`, issue #2456 (owner, 2026-10-07: "1y, 2y, 3y, 4y"). On a PUSH to `main` only; on any other event it is skipped and nothing waits for it. A merge-button merge of an up-to-date PR carries a tree CI has already tested. `verdict-reuse.sh` looks up the runs of this workflow on the merged head (the merge commit's second parent) and answers `reuse=true` only when one concluded `success`, ran every job a reuse would skip, and tested exactly this tree: for a `pull_request` run, the `tested-tree:` its Task_QaWorkingCopy job wrote into its check run's summary; for a dispatch, the head's own tree. Then the four `bun test` shards (part of Task_TypeScript), the three e2e shards (Task_E2E) and the standalone ratchet (part of Task_RepositoryGates) are skipped on this push, and the summary names the run whose verdict stands. Everything that judges the tree against `main` or reads `qa-reports` still runs. A squash, an API error, a missing record or a mismatch is `reuse=false` and every job runs: could-not-determine is never green. Drawn before the fork because the jobs it can skip wait for it; the others do not. Since the same ruling, a newer push to `main` also cancels an older main run still in progress (the workflow's `concurrency`), so main's verdict history is thinned by decision.

terms.prefLabel: Record the verdict on the node
terms.definition: Findings are advice, not commits — the same separation the generic reviewer lane keeps. Record them where the next reader meets the node.

Does the node declare what KIND of node it is? Does a widened type carry its mirrors? Does a removed field leave a reason behind, so the next author does not re-add it in good faith? And where the node RENDERS to something the site serves — a colour, a glyph, a theme's tokens — does a Tool maintain that artefact, and does the visual fact have only one home? The node decides; the stylesheet reports.

Does it name skills, and do they resolve? Is the mechanism it advertises the one that actually runs? Are its IRIs minted rather than written out? And the question a covered skill hides: is the COMMAND reachable, or only the skill satisfied? A skill can be served by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from no node, and check:tools reports it as covered and is right to.
`check:tools`, `kg:audit` and `typecheck`. Read the kg-qa sidecar rather than the summary: it is written per node so an inherited defect and a new one are distinguishable.

terms.prefLabel: Accept it, and record where it came from
terms.definition: Both branches land here. An unprompted offer is accepted as it stands — do not make somebody follow a process to hand over what they already have. Provenance is recorded whichever channel it arrived through: a description given in chat has a source and can be wrong, exactly as a PDF does.

terms.prefLabel: Ask for a link or a description
terms.definition: Both forms, named together. A person who cannot find the file often knows exactly what it is, and a description in their own words is an acquired resource rather than a consolation prize. Asking for the upload first demands the one thing they may not have, before the cheaper answers have been offered. Say what happens if they do nothing.

Composed from the declaration by the `upload-url` Tool, never written by hand: the queue is declared with INSTANCE scope, and a forge URL needs the path relative to the REPOSITORY. Every failure is named — no origin remote, a non-GitHub forge, a declared-but-absent queue — because a URL is believed, and somebody sent to a wrong one cannot tell it from an empty directory. On failure, fall back to the conversation.

terms.prefLabel: Route it, and watch the queue
terms.definition: A file goes to ingestion; a link or a description goes to whatever will resolve it. Acquisition stops here — the moment a file is in the queue, library-ingestion owns it, and keeping that seam sharp is what lets a resource acquired through a channel that does not exist yet reach ingestion unchanged. An arrival may be minutes or days away, so it is watched rather than chased.

terms.prefLabel: Give a link, a description, or neither
terms.definition: "Or neither" is a real outcome, not a failure. The ask says what happens if nothing comes, and then that happens — the work proceeds without the resource and says so.

terms.prefLabel: Drop the file in the queue
terms.definition: Through the forge's upload form, a commit, or any other route that lands the file in the declared queue. The agent watches rather than chases: an arrival may be minutes or days away.

terms.prefLabel: Select upstream asset and target folio
terms.definition: Name the upstream instance (`<owner>/<repo>`), the asset's declared path in that instance, the commit `ref` (when pinned), and the target folio declaration that will receive the copy.

terms.prefLabel: Copy asset into target folio and declare in assets[]
terms.definition: Write the asset bytes into a declared path inside the target folio and add the `KgAsset` entry to the target folio's `<name>.json` `assets[]` list (`directory-conventions`). Never drop the copy into an undeclared scratch directory.

terms.prefLabel: Browse in place, emit a KgAsset snippet
terms.definition: Clean degradation when no write capability (`git-push`, `github-api`, `github-connector`) is present: inspect the asset in place through the zero-write `browse` affordance and output the ready-to-paste `KgAsset` entry (with `source: { instance, path, ref }` populated) so the author can apply it where they have write access.

Check whether the session holds at least one of the three write capabilities (`git-push`, `github-api`, or `github-connector` under `scenarios/capabilities/`). Keep available, absent and could-not-determine distinct.

Read the asset bytes and its origin coordinates (`instance` as `<owner>/<repo>`, `path` within that instance, and commit `ref`) from the source knowledge graph without modifying anything in the source lane.

Populate `source: { instance, path, ref }` (`AssetSourceSchema` in `schemas/kg/kg-node.ts`) on the new `KgAsset` entry in the same change. Because `source` absent is a third state meaning "authored locally in this instance", omitting `source` on a copied asset is forbidden.

Run `bun run cat check:declaration-resolution` (`check:declared-assets`) to verify that the copied asset exists at its declared path, its `KgAsset.source` conforms to `AssetSourceSchema`, and the upstream source graph remains untouched.

terms.prefLabel: Edit, comment or raise todos on the folio's copy
terms.definition: The copied asset is now writable content of the target folio with recorded upstream provenance (`KgAsset.source`). The folio author may edit it in place, attach review comments, or raise todos (`todo-manager`) against it.

terms.prefLabel: Edit it in place — it is your own content
terms.definition: The ordinary path, drawn so the process does not read as though every edit needs a copy. Content in a writable directory is authored content and is edited where it lives; the copy-out is for somebody else's bytes, not for yours.

terms.prefLabel: Land the bytes in the copier's own folio/
terms.definition: Into the copier's own declared `folio/`, never a scratch area — a directory nobody declared is a directory nobody gates, and the copy would be publishable by accident. The copy is NOT read-only: it is the copier's own content, makes no claim about anybody else's bytes, and freezing it too would mean the next person needs a copy of the copy.

terms.prefLabel: Read the original — and write nothing
terms.definition: A read, and the only interaction this process has with the source. Its digest and `provenance` are carried forward: the digest so Task_VerifySourceUntouched has something to check against, and `provenance` so the copy can name what it came out of without re-deriving it.

terms.prefLabel: Record what this is a copy of
terms.definition: The step that is easy to omit and impossible to reconstruct afterwards. `provenance` is a PAIR: `upstream` is the remote thing, `local` is the original in this repository. A copy-out writes `local`; it does not overwrite `upstream`, and it does not reuse `upstream` for a local value. Without `local`, one rename later the copy is indistinguishable from original work and nothing downstream can repair it, because the information was never written down.

terms.prefLabel: Verify the ORIGINAL still hashes to its digest
terms.definition: `check:materialized-fixity`. Run against the SOURCE, not the copy — the copy is new content with no claim to verify, and the source is the thing a botched copy-out would have disturbed. A mismatch here means the copy-out was an edit in place wearing a copy's clothes, and it is the only signal that tells the two apart.

Recognise the request as a platform capability change rather than content work, from crdm-detect's signals. Never call it "CRDM" to the person. Mid-content-work, ask whether to pause for requirements now or record a work item for later — do not switch on your own.
The BA describes the capability gap in their own words. They do not need to know it is called CRDM.
The stakeholders sign off, the BA confirms every criterion is met, and only then does the agent close the issue. Never the other way round: an agent must never assume completion.

Between requirements and sign-off, and the order is the argument: requirements are statements about things, and the model says what the things ARE. Drafted earlier it is invented from nothing, since the entities come from the phase-2 BPA; drafted later, sign-off approves requirements whose nouns were never pinned — which is how two stakeholders approve one sentence meaning different things.

One phase and not three, because the loops say so: an increment the BA rejects, an MVP that is not ready, and stakeholder findings all route back into implementation. A subprocess has one exit and cannot be re-entered once finished, so splitting this region would have changed what the diagram says.

terms.prefLabel: Link the work to an issue
terms.definition: Feature work must be linked to a GitHub issue. Scan before creating, and never create one without the BA's permission — an issue is the stakeholder's record, not the agent's scratchpad.

Identify the stakeholders, synthesise a needs statement from the sources, and loop until the BA and the stakeholders both recognise it. The loop is the phase: a needs statement nobody confirmed is an agent's summary, not a requirement.
Map the current workflow, then define the requirements and the impact they carry, and loop until approved. Same shape as Phase 1 and for the same reason: an unapproved requirement is a proposal.

The approved requirements become work-plan items, the BA signs off, and the branch is announced on the issue. The announcement is on the single edge into delivery, so the three loops back into implementation do not re-announce.

terms.prefLabel: Close issue ONLY on BA authorisation
terms.definition: Reachable only through BA_Confirm, which is the BA saying every criterion is met. An agent must never close an issue without that explicit authorisation — the gate is the preceding task, and this name says so rather than leaving a reader to trace the flow for it.

THE RECORD, and not relaxable, because a judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from one never made (`adjudication`, A_RecordEntry). Append one `requirement-signoff` record to `test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set slug>.attestations.json` — who (kind, id, actor), at, scope (the set or one member), the outcome from the requirement-set code list, the stage it moves the set to, the reason, and the permalink to the issue comment where it was decided — and set the set's `stage` to match. GW_SignoffRecorded after this reads the record back, so this step cannot be skipped by completing it: a sign-off that left no attestation loops here again.

The business analyst confirms every acceptance criterion from the requirements is met. The issue closes only on their authorisation — an agent never closes an issue on its own say-so. It IS an adjudication with the requirement-set answers: an approval here moves the set to `accepted`, which `check:requirements` refuses unless it is a human's and every approved member is `in-force`.

Phase 6's "explicit confirmation before merging to main", made a step that can refuse. Once per pull request the feature still has open, after the sign-off is recorded and before the issue is closed: an issue is not closed on a feature that is not on `main`. `merge-to-main.bpmn` reads each head's evidence live, establishes that the owner authorised THAT merge (a stakeholder sign-off or the BA's confirmation is acceptance of the feature, not authorisation to merge it, unless the owner's own words say so), records the authorisation, merges, and confirms the base. A PR the owner holds or refuses stays open, and A_Close then waits: the BA's authorisation to close does not cover a feature that did not land. An increment the owner asked to land earlier in Phase 6 went through the same sub-process at that time.
Stakeholders sign off on the delivered feature on the issue, having tested the built artefact rather than a description of it.

terms.prefLabel: Declare the model where a tool can read it
terms.definition: A model in prose is a proposal; a model in the declaration is a model. Ship a reader in the same change: a model that is only documentation goes inert.

terms.prefLabel: Identify entities from the BPA and requirements
terms.definition: Every verb in the BPA whose object is a candidate entity, and every noun in a requirement. An entity with no identifier is an attribute of something else — that test is decisive and belongs to the technique skill.

Stated in both directions, because "one attestation per report" and "one report per attestation" are different claims and a model with only the first cannot say whether a re-signature is an update or a second row.

terms.prefLabel: Confirm the entities are the ones meant
terms.definition: A naming question. The BA owns the domain vocabulary; the agent does not guess, which is CRDM's own rule for phase 1 and applies here with more force.
An operational question, asked of the people who run the process because they know where the exceptions are.

terms.prefLabel: Audit the code nodes the increment adds
terms.definition: Descend into the review task for what this increment CHANGED IN THE GRAPH — Tool definitions in `tools/` and schema definition nodes under `schemas/`. It runs before the summary, and therefore before an MVP can be shared: a Tool or schema node shipped in an MVP is the version stakeholders start building expectations on, and a node that names a skill nobody wrote is cheaper to catch here than after sign-off. Called, not inherited: the agent keeps its implementing role and takes on the `code-reviewer` lane inside Process_CodeReview for that call path only.

An MVP is shared AS A branches/ DEPLOY, not as a description of one. `feature-staging.yml` publishes the branch under `branches/<branch-slug>/` on gh-pages and comments the URL on the PR, so the stakeholder who tests it is looking at the built artefact rather than at a screenshot — the same argument the merge discipline makes about rendered work: holding a rendered change back for assessment makes assessment harder, not safer.

Inner loop: agent claims a bean, implements on feature branch, opens PR, posts summary to the issue. When the requirement changes a rendered surface, implement against the wireframe candidate the requester or BA chose in Phases 3–4 (Process_WireframeDesignReview, called from Process_CRDM_Requirements), not against a fresh design; and the delivery summary links the chosen candidate beside the after-screenshot, so the reviewer can see the build matches what was approved.
What was accomplished, what remains, and the staging links: one deep link per changed page on the preview, with the same page on main (staging-review, "The deep-link rule").
Inner loop: the BA tests each delivered increment against the acceptance criteria. They do not review code — they test behaviour.
Outer loop: the BA presents the accumulated increments to stakeholders as a testable MVP. Staging URL, demo, or walkthrough.
The BA translates stakeholder findings into actionable direction: new beans or bean updates for the agent.

On the single edge from `Start_Process_CRDM_Deliver` into `A_Implement`, so the approach is chosen before any code exists. By Phase 6 the needs, requirements and data model are signed off, which is exactly the evidence an options analysis needs and the reason it belongs here rather than earlier: at `Call_Needs` there is nothing to weigh, and after `A_Implement` the choice has been made in code. The three loop-backs into `A_Implement` — `_5` (increment rejected), `_7` (MVP not ready), `_13` (feedback translated) — deliberately BYPASS this call. Routing them through it would run the subprocess on every iteration of the inner loop, which is the ceremony this design refuses: a gate invoked on every pass stops being read. An iteration reworks an approach already chosen; if the APPROACH is what is wrong, that is not a loop iteration and it belongs to the calling step in `crdm-requirements.bpmn`. Contrast `upstream-version-adoption`, where the loop DOES re-enter the analysis. There the loop-back returns to `A_Impact`, which re-gathers the evidence, so the second pass weighs genuinely different inputs. Here the loop returns to implementation with the evidence unchanged. `A_Implement` carries a `note` on the bean (its claim is the OPEN that `Process_CRDM` calls first); this step carries no bean op, because `Process_OptionsAnalysis` ends with its own `decision-audit` note on the bean the caller claimed.
Stakeholders test the delivered feature in their own workflow, with their own data. They report what works and what does not.

terms.prefLabel: Ask BA to create or link issue
terms.definition: Ask — never create. Creating an issue without the BA's permission is the thing this step exists to prevent.
A match was found: ask the person whether the requirements go on #NNN, then link the work there. The issue is where stakeholders sign off, so no phase proceeds without one.
Search open issues, then recently closed ones, by title and body keywords for one this request belongs to. Requirements may span several issues; note every relevant one.

When the requirement is initiated or updated through a human-agent chat, search the beans and the repository's issues and open PRs for relevance, categorize and summarize them, and ask the user whether and how to coordinate. Judgement decides the categories; the user decides the coordination.
The agent asks the BA who is affected by this change. The BA knows the domain — the agent does not guess.

From the chat, issue, uploads and library sources, write a clear, jargon-free statement of what is needed and why, tied to a concrete workflow. Post it on the GitHub issue, not in chat, and ask the requester and stakeholders to review it.
The BA reviews what the agent synthesised and checks it against what they actually need.
Stakeholders confirm, on the issue, that the needs statement says what they need — or say what to change. A stakeholder's judgement; an agent does not record it for them.

Phase 4 often ends with a CHOICE rather than a plan, and this is the step that hands it over. Per option: what it does, its pro, its con, what it changes DOWNSTREAM, and how reversible it is — laid out where the rows can be read against each other, then one recommendation and a stated default. A step of its own rather than a line inside A_DefineReqs, because it has a different output and a different reader: the impact analysis is for the record, the comparison is the thing the BA answers from. Folding it in is how it gets skipped — the analysis feels finished, so the options go over as a list of names. When Call_Wireframe ran, its wireframe candidates are among the options: one row per candidate, with a link to its web and mobile screenshots. Skipped legitimately when the analysis yields ONE viable approach. Do not manufacture alternatives to fill a table.

Two skills, because this step is two things: the requirements come from the CRDM process, the impact half is a question about the entities and relations the change touches, which is what data modelling answers; a folio-content skill such as `content-graph` is not one this harness diagram can bind.
Business-process analysis here means reading the existing diagrams under processes/ and drawing the gap, so the skill that implements this step is the BPMN one.

The BA reviews the formal requirements and the impact analysis the agent produced. When a requirement changes a rendered surface, the BA (or the requester) also reviews the wireframe candidates, web and mobile, shown wherever the requester will look (the conversation, the issue, the pull request, or several) with staging deep links and screenshots, and chooses one before implementation starts. The agent records the choice; it never makes it.

Design use of wireframe-design-review, before implementation: a written design intent, at least two mid-fidelity candidates each with a web and a mobile layout, the mechanical checks, and a blind review. The candidates are committed as assets of the request's proposal, under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ beside docs/proposals/<slug>.md, on the feature branch so feature-staging publishes them, and shown where the requester will look, chosen from context — the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or several of these — each place carrying the same staging deep links and screenshots (staging-review, the deep-link rule, point 5: where it goes is a judgement). The requester or BA is the human reviewer and chooses one at BA_ReviewReqs. A wireframe is part of the design process for adjudication (methodologies/wiregen.md). The candidates ARE the options A_CompareOptions lays out, so this merges into it rather than producing a second comparison.

Stakeholders approve the requirements and impact analysis on the issue, or send them back for revision. Only their approval moves the work to sign-off; an agent never records an approval on a person's behalf.

terms.prefLabel: Announce the branch on the issue
terms.definition: On CREATING the feature branch, comment on the issue: the branch name, the process and phase, and the beans claimed. Visibility is the whole point — without it a sibling session or a human cannot tell that work has begun, only that it has finished. Deliberately on this edge and not inside Phase 6. The three loops back into A_Implement (increment rejected, MVP not ready, feedback translated) re-enter implementation on the SAME branch, and re-announcing on each would be noise. Announce once, when the branch is created. Before announcing, run the collision review that starts any new unit of work (coordinate, "Starting new work"): open PRs and in-progress beans checked against the branch's files and subject, scaled to the blast radius, and the result recorded in the bean before the first edit.

The agent mints the implementation beans itself with `beans create`, running the exact-title existence check first. The engine has no `create` op — it claims, notes and resolves the instance's OWN bean — so what this step records here is a note that the plan now exists.

terms.prefLabel: Offer KG destinations for the agreed set
terms.definition: Without this step, agreed and signed-off requirements exist only as an issue and a conversation, and the knowledge graph never learns them. ONE question for the SET, not one per requirement: a six-phase run can agree many, and asking six times is the same failure as a form that re-asks what it was already told. The options are DERIVED from the graphs this instance declares in `<name>.json`, read at the time of asking, so an instance that adds a graph gets it in the offer without anybody editing a skill. Never a list typed from memory.

The offer produces a DECISION, not a node. `placement` then decides instance, graph and node kind — it is the step that catches a hardcoded path or a literal naming one folio — and the authoring itself becomes a bean, because work here is a bean before it is a file. `op="note"` and not `create`, for the reason `A_CreateBeans` above states: the engine has no `create` op — it claims, notes and resolves the instance's OWN bean. The agent mints the authoring bean itself with `beans create`, running the exact-title existence check first, and what this step records is a note that the decision was taken.

THE RECORD, and not relaxable, because a judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from one never made (`adjudication`, A_RecordEntry). Append one `requirement-signoff` record to `test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set slug>.attestations.json` — who (kind, id, actor), at, scope (the set or one member), the outcome from the requirement-set code list, the stage it moves the set to, the reason, and the permalink to the issue comment where it was decided — and set the set's `stage` to match. GW_SignoffRecorded after this reads the record back, so this step cannot be skipped by completing it: a sign-off that left no attestation loops here again.

A PERSON'S STEP, and `none` is one of the answers rather than a refusal to answer. A requirement whose whole content is carried by the code becomes a commit and nothing else; a graph that acquires a node for it is a graph with a node nobody will ever read. The default creates NOTHING. An agent that decides on its own that a requirement "is really a skill" has manufactured a node nobody asked for, in a graph somebody else maintains — which is what this step exists to prevent.

The business analyst / requester signs off on the agreed requirement set, on the issue: what was agreed and what was deferred. Recorded as their decision, with its reason, never by an agent on their behalf. It IS an adjudication: it calls Process_Adjudication with the requirement-set answers, and every answer goes through A_RecordSignoff before anything follows it.

terms.prefLabel: Grant a dispensation, with its reason
terms.definition: The rule applies and this subject is a stated exception. A `kind: "human"` entry with `result: "pass"` overrides the script's `fail` for that criterion, and ONLY while its `field_hash` matches the current source — so the dispensation is scoped to the version it was granted against, lapses when the block changes, and never becomes precedent. There is nothing to overturn later; the source moving overturns it. A dispensation with no `notes` is not a dispensation. It is an override somebody applied to get to green, and nobody can review it afterwards — which is why this step is not relaxable.

terms.prefLabel: Write the entry that LEADS — keeping the checker's beneath it
terms.definition: Not relaxable, and the one step here that is not. A judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a checker that was never run, so the judgement is free and the record is not. Do not resolve the disagreement away: both entries stay, the adjudication on top under the sweep's most-recent-matching-hash rule. A disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information, and somebody re-running the check next month needs to find that a checker read it differently rather than a clean pass. `/api/relevance/adjudicate` reached the same rule independently — `human_adjudicated` written alongside, never over, the agent's `assessed_by`.

terms.prefLabel: Scope the criterion so it stops applying here
terms.definition: One edit to the criterion rather than ten overrules on the blocks it should never have covered. This branch is the one an adjudicator under time pressure converts into a dispensation, and the conversion is a defect: a dispensation lapses when the source moves, so a mis-scoped criterion granted its way past comes back every time anybody touches the block.

The shared judgement — entry condition, untainted dispatch, person-or-agent restriction — asked with THIS question's permitted answers. `cat-harness.processes:adjudication codes` sits here rather than on `A_Adjudicate` inside it because the answers depend on what was asked, and the gateway below is what acts on them: the engine refuses a mismatch between the two. `Process_Adjudication` may also leave at `End_NotAdjudicable` — one entry and no other side is a review or a gate, not a disagreement — in which case nothing below runs and there is nothing to record.
Process_PublishAlert — the ONE alert every failing step after the publish button goes through, whichever step it was.

`compose-docs.ts` composes the docs layers into one Jekyll source (`cat-harness/docs/` as the base, the checkout root's `docs/` laid over it); then each instance that builds a site of its own composes it into that source at `<instance>/`, so the result is one site with one sidebar, search and language selector. The step is bound by the Tool, not by a `calledElement`: the step names skill `docs-generation`, each Tool that satisfies it and composes a site lists its own `subprocesses`, and those carry the steps; which instances compose a site is data in their declarations. A composing Tool may name a post-build pass, which `Task_Build` runs after the Jekyll build. With nothing to compose, the source is left as `compose-docs` wrote it, and that is reported.

Process_PublishVerification: the verifier set over the built tree (`publish-verify.ts`), before the deploy. Its outcome is recorded, not acted on: the deploy goes ahead, and `Task_Judge` judges it after the push.

terms.prefLabel: Build the Jekyll site and the API reference
terms.definition: Builds the composed source with Jekyll 4 and just-the-docs (`bundle exec jekyll build`), runs each composing Tool's post-build pass, mounts instance-rendered content (`mount-instance-docs.ts`), and generates the TypeScript API reference with TypeDoc (`.github/actions/typedoc-api`). The main deploy is a full build: every index is rebuilt from the tree being published. See skill `feature-staging`, section Build types.

terms.prefLabel: Close the publication manager's alert, if open
terms.definition: A clean publish resolves whatever the last failure raised: close the open publication-manager tracking issue with a comment naming this run.

terms.prefLabel: Export the knowledge graph and its schema
terms.definition: Exports the knowledge graph and its schema into the published tree (`kg-export.ts`, `harness-schema-export.ts`, `kg-viewer.ts`), stripping the unpublished graph typologies, then runs the built-site checks: every maintained artefact is present (`bun run cat check:maintained-artefacts`), no block-level markup escaped (`check:escaped-markup`), the QA witnesses and results are published, and the navbar tiles resolve. Each outcome is recorded, not acted on: `Task_Judge` judges them after the push.

Reads the outcomes `Task_Export` and `Call_Verify` recorded (maintained artefacts, escaped markup, QA witnesses and results, navbar tiles, the export verification) and fails the run if any failed. The site is already live, so a failure here means a published site with a known problem, not a withheld one.

Calls Process_RenderKgToCdn with the built tree, the site root as publication root URL, and GitHub Pages as target, so its `gh-pages` Tool (`publish-gh-pages.sh`) replaces the branch and returns the push's status and message. A status other than `pushed` takes `no` at Did the deploy succeed?.

terms.prefLabel: Regenerate every derived reference from its source
terms.definition: Regenerates every derived reference from its source, so the site is never built from committed copies that may be stale: the derived artefacts kept off the commit (`bun run cat derive:publish`), the skill schema and instruction pages (`gen-schema-docs.ts`, `gen-skill-docs.ts`), the content-backed docs pages (`gen-docs-pages.ts`), the graph projections and viewers (`schema:viz`, `library:viz`, `uploads:viz`, `voices:viz` and others), the handler and translation indexes (`handler:index`, `translation:index`), and the BPMN drawings and process pages (`render:bpmn`, `processes:viz`). After a main deploy, `writer-records` reruns every writer and QA step under strace to record its reads, so a preview reruns only those whose reads changed; the main deploy runs everything.

terms.prefLabel: Restore the OPEN PRs' staging previews
terms.definition: Copies every open pull request's `branches/<slug>/` preview from `gh-pages` into the publish directory before the replace, once per publish attempt (`restore-staging.ts`, run inside `publish-gh-pages.sh`). Only open PRs' previews are carried; a branch that cannot be read refuses the publish.

`bun run cat security:gate`, before the site is built. It runs every security check the repository names: workflow injection, secret leaks, lockfile and toolchain pins, QA reviewer permission, materialised fixity, and third-party action SHA pinning outside staging-only workflows. Each reports pass, fail or unknown; a blocking fail or unknown refuses the publish.

terms.prefLabel: Repeat the slug, exactly, to confirm
terms.definition: The one step in this process that is a person's. Repeating the slug is not ceremony: it names the artefact being confirmed, so a confirmation cannot be inherited by a later run pointed at a different preview.

Build the preview from the PR's head: regenerate the generated docs, trim what this preview does not need, render the BPMN diagrams, then Jekyll, TypeDoc and the knowledge-graph export, with the staging banner and SEO identity claims stripped. It is a PREVIEW build (CAT_BUILD_TYPE=preview, owner 2026-11-01): only what the change reaches, and every whole-corpus index (builtAtPublish entries marked index: true, and the search index) is main's copy, put back rather than rebuilt. A branch frozen for public comment is dispatched with build_type: full instead. Skill feature-staging, section Build types. A PREVIEW REBUILDS ONLY ITS DEPENDENCY CONE (owner cards Q-CONE-1 C and Q-CONE-2 B, 2026-11-01): main's writer records say what each derive:publish writer and each step of the QA working copy READ. A writer or QA step whose recorded reads all match is not run, and main's outputs for it are put back. Every other one runs. QA is not left out of a preview, only narrowed to what the change can reach. Inside a preview's QA build, `skill:register` also leaves to derive:publish the two pages that derive:publish builds anyway and that no later QA step reads (`skills:docs` and `lsi:viz`), so they are built once.

terms.prefLabel: Comment the preview URL on the PR
terms.definition: Post, or update in place, one comment on the PR giving the preview URL (branches/<slug>/) and the commit it was built from. Pull-request events only.

terms.prefLabel: Push to the CDN under branches/
terms.definition: A PREVIEW IS THE GENERAL STEP WITH A DIFFERENT ROOT (owner, 2026-09-30: "independent of staging vs publication … just rendering"). Process_RenderKgToCdn, entered with the tree Task_Build rendered, `branches/<slug>/` under the site root as the publication root URL, and GitHub Pages as the target, so its `gh-pages` Tool pushes. For this target the push is `keep_files: true` with a `destination_dir`, so it adds one directory beside whatever else is on the branch; it is also RETRIED once: five other workflows push to `gh-pages` without joining this one's concurrency group, and a queue does not help because GitHub CANCELS a pending job when a newer one arrives for the same group rather than queueing it. Measured 2026-09-19: three staging runs from three different branches inside 17 seconds, two cancelled. The call returns the push's status and message; the render log and the PR comment that follow are this process's own. THE PREVIEW CAP rides in the same commit (owner ruling 2026-10-02, issue #1868: "cap the maximum number of previews (<= 10) and rotate old ones off", amended 2026-10-04 to a SIZE budget: "Cap by size, not count", "3gb"): `staging-rotate.ts` keeps this preview plus the most recently updated others while their total fits MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES = 3 GB and removes the rest, oldest first, each with a `removed` render-log entry and its record retired into branches/_retired/. Every push attempt re-reads `gh-pages` and re-decides rather than rebasing, so a lost race never pushes a stale removal. A rotated-off preview is regenerated by the next push to its PR branch.

Its OWN commit, not part of the deploy. The publish action writes only into `destination_dir`, so an entry riding in `_site` would land at `branches/<slug>/_render-log/` — inside the directory a cleanup removes, which is the one place a record of the removal must not be. `continue-on-error`: a preview that deployed and whose entry did not is a gap in the record, not a failed deploy.

terms.prefLabel: Post the retention notice on the PR
terms.definition: Removal was not confirmed, so the preview stays: post a retention notice on the PR giving its URL and saying it has NOT been removed, and the two ways to remove it: the staging:cleanup label while the PR is open, or, once it is closed, a Run workflow dispatch with cleanup_slug and a matching cleanup_confirm.

Re-evaluated AT REMOVAL TIME, through the same `previewLiveness` the health sweep uses rather than a second implementation of it. The sweep runs daily and proposes; this acts. Between them a branch can come back to life — bean `w2g5` documents exactly that, a session reusing one branch across five successive pull requests.

terms.prefLabel: Remove the preview and log it
terms.definition: ONE COMMIT for the removal and its record. A separate log push can fail on its own and leave a preview that vanished with nothing saying why — which is the exact state bean `plj1` left the branch in. `render-log.ts` refuses a `removed` entry with no reason, so this step fails loudly rather than writing a record that says an artefact went and not why.

terms.prefLabel: Remove it AND append `removed` — one commit
terms.definition: Say what is going — size and file count — then remove branches/<slug>/ and append `removed` to the render log in the SAME commit, so a preview cannot vanish without a record of who dispatched it and why. The slug is a dispatch input, so the tool re-checks it by value rather than trusting the guard.

terms.prefLabel: Derive the slug from the head ref
terms.definition: Derive the slug from the PR's head ref: every character outside [a-zA-Z0-9._-] becomes '-', runs of '-' collapse, and leading or trailing '-' is trimmed. It must be one safe path segment, checked by value.

terms.prefLabel: Check the slug and its confirmation
terms.definition: Guarded three ways because a dispatch input is a DELETION TRIGGER. `workflow_dispatch` is available only to an actor with write access; the slug must match exactly the characters the sed pipeline can produce, with `.` and `..` refused by name; and the confirmation must repeat the slug, so a confirmation cannot be carried over from an earlier run against a different preview.

terms.prefLabel: Regenerate from the source and diff
terms.definition: Run the caller's generator with --check: regenerate the file from its source in memory and diff it against the committed copy. Several independent generators run in one job are still one step, because they have no order between them.
The one step no package may relax. A repository cut changes the substrate every other diagram's lanes bind to, and that is a person's decision.

terms.prefLabel: Brief the topic before touching anything
terms.definition: What am I doing and why is it worth doing; what do I already know, with each measurement's provenance; how do I plan to do it and WHAT WOULD FALSIFY THE APPROACH. A falsifier that never fires is decoration.

A `<name>.json` entry with its `graphs[]` kinds. A sub-graph that owns its own layout gains a NESTED declaration whose paths resolve against its own directory, so the whole graph relocates by moving one folder.

terms.prefLabel: 4 · Extract — a directory move, not a file-by-file sift
terms.definition: Only once edges are zero and the declaration stands alone: move the sub-graph out as one directory move, not a file-by-file sift. Its nested declaration resolves paths against its own directory, so moving the folder moves the graph. The five-point gate is in migration-plan.md Phase II.

Only once cross-edges measure zero: give the sub-graph its own declaration, its own namespace and its own published artefact, as bootstrap/ has (its own declaration, bs: namespace and graph document). Nothing moves yet; the sub-graph now stands alone in place.

`bun run cat check:partition`. Read the unassigned column before the edge count, and quote BOTH numbers rather than only the one that improved. The edge count can rise when the measurement improves (previously unjudged edges are folded in); that is correct.

terms.prefLabel: 2b · Prune, merge, factor — or the classification is wrong
terms.definition: The only four moves. Move the shared TARGET first and the importers after; check the target's layer before the importer's; a schema moves with its script. The fix is never an exemption, it is the right owner.

terms.prefLabel: Report what would move — sizes, and what breaks
terms.definition: The agent reports and waits: what would move, how large, what in the parent breaks, and the rollback. `deletion-requires-confirmation` is not a courtesy to waive: an agent never removes or relocates a durable artefact on its own initiative.

The sibling's ask, unchanged in letters and recommendation, through `Process_AskThePerson`: the full chat text first, naming the sibling and that the answer will be passed on, then the card. A tap on the sibling's own card or a Blue-column answer in the sheet answers it too; take the first.
Say it comes from the sibling (title and link) and give the context or result in full. State `informed`.

Chat copies keep their text: the question struck through and "[Edit: <letter> chosen by <who>, <time>]" added. Cards closed with the chosen option. The sheet's "Decision needed" block replaced by the decision and who made it. Withdrawn or superseded hand-backs marked the same way, with the reason.
On `answerRoute`, with the person's own message attached by id where the host allows, so the sibling can treat it as the person's approval. A paraphrase is never approval.
Never ask the person again for what they answered. A rule-level answer goes into the governing skill in the same turn.

terms.prefLabel: Compose the hand-back and post it in own thread
terms.definition: Compose it once, against the input schema: a question is the full ask-the-person input (what will differ, context, lettered options with a one-line trade-off each, the recommendation, what happens with no answer); context, a result or a blocker gets the same stand-alone test. Post it in your own thread too, chat text then card. Your own thread is never the only copy.

terms.prefLabel: Hand it back to the discussion agent
terms.definition: By the host's route: `message_coordinator` or `message_thread` in Claude projects; the final report (a json block valid against the input schema) for a subagent; `SendMessage` for a sibling session. Then keep working on the recommended option where it can be undone, or stop if `blocking`.

terms.prefLabel: Mirror it to the feedback channel
terms.definition: Review sheet: the "Decision needed" block in the row's agent column, Agentic status `Needs you` (the document layer's `review-sheet-script` skill). Issue or PR: a comment. An extra copy, never instead of the discussion.

terms.prefLabel: Draw the board of todos and beans
terms.definition: The todo board mounts inside the landing board, so harness cards and todo stickies share one surface. Each card carries an edit link only when the build composed one.
The theme art for that harness's pages, all three crops or none, and the URL scopes that make a page that harness's (`pageGround`). The site owner's ground is the fallback for a page no scope claims.
Through whichever write tool the session has. The change is a proposal: it goes into the content change review, which decides whether it is published.

terms.prefLabel: Publish docs on their theme's art
terms.definition: `head_custom.html` sets the ground behind every page of the harness, under two scrims of the page's own colour, so text and links keep the plain page's contrast.

terms.prefLabel: Read a page or a card
terms.definition: The floor of the interface: everything a harness publishes can be read with no account and no tool.

terms.prefLabel: Compose each harness's nav and tile
terms.definition: One themed section per instance in dependency order, from its declaration: its docs, its declared subgraphs (a graph with no viewer is shown inert and labelled), and its theme. Written to `_data/harness.json` by `sync-docs-harness.ts`.
With no write tool the reader's point is not lost: it is recorded as feedback for someone who can write.

For WHO SMART Guidelines content, automatically appends the WHO legal disclaimer: - Translation not created by WHO - English edition is authoritative original - WHO not responsible for translation accuracy Only applies when folio contentType includes WHO/DAK content.

The coordinator assigns the translation to a qualified translator, ideally a domain SME for the content area. For WHO content, the translator should be familiar with WHO SMART Guidelines terminology. The assignment includes: - The .pot file(s) from extraction - The domain glossary - Context notes (block kind, chapter, content area) - The deadline

Verify that all msgid entries have msgstr translations. Partial translations are acceptable for initial submissions but must be flagged for follow-up. The coordinator checks: - % of strings translated - Any fuzzy-flagged entries - Missing critical sections

Scan the source content and write the translatable strings to .pot files at the configured granularity: segment prose by paragraph, shield what must not be translated (math, code, labels, Lean companions) as placeholders, normalise whitespace, and extract metadata such as titles, alt text and captions. Tool: the translation_extract MCP tool.
The coordinator selects: - Which content nodes need translation (block, section, chapter, or folio) - The target locale (one of the supportedLocales in <name>.config.json) - The priority and deadline

Read the .po file and the source .md, substitute msgstr for msgid, unshield the placeholders, and write the translated .md to translations/<locale>/. Check structure (paragraph count, heading levels) and completeness (no empty msgstr), and lint (doubled punctuation, orphaned placeholders). Tool: the translation_inject MCP tool.

Builds the locale term base for the target locale from the layered glossaries, has it reviewed, and hands it to the translator with the POT. Each layer's glossary is the directory it declares with the `glossary` graph typology. Precedence, within one subject area (the scheme's `subject`): the more authoritative (lower) layer fixes a term's translation; an instance layer only adds, and may not give a fixed term a second translation. A match in another subject area is a sense check for the reviewer, not a violation. Previous translations of related content are evidence for a term with no fixed form, not a source that overrides one. A fixed translation is an authored term with a non-empty, non-fuzzy msgstr in its scheme's catalogue (translation-manager, "The locale term base").

The translator receives: - .pot file with source strings (msgid) - Domain glossary with approved term translations - Context notes per string - Style guide and WHO terminology references Tools: Poedit, Weblate, Crowdin, or direct .po editing.
Return to the translator with a list of untranslated or fuzzy strings that need attention.

The reviewer annotates specific passages that need correction and returns to the translator with detailed feedback. Each annotation includes: - The passage in question - What is wrong (terminology, meaning, style) - The suggested correction or reference

Back-translate the target-language .md into the source language and compare the meaning with the original. It catches semantic drift and terminology misses that a forward-only fluency check cannot see, and tells the two apart. Tool: the translation_validate MCP tool. No gateway follows: drift or clean, the translation goes to Task_SMEReview with the findings attached. Which of two readings is right is a human call (translation-manager, "route drift to a human reviewer"), and every translation in this workflow is reviewed and signed off anyway, so a clean result is evidence for the reviewer and never a way around them. The findings include `translation:glossary:check`'s: every glossary term translated against the locale term base, fixed before sign-off, with its glossary section in the KG QA report.

The reviewer signs off the translation, making it official. This records: - signedOffBy: the reviewer's identity - signedOffAt: the current timestamp - sourceHash: SHA-256 of the source .md - level: block | section | chapter | folio Tool: translation_signoff MCP tool

A subject-matter expert reviews the injected translated markdown for: - Clinical/technical accuracy of terminology - Preservation of meaning from the source - Cultural appropriateness for the target locale - Consistency with the domain glossary For WHO content: the SME verifies that normative statements ("SHALL", "SHOULD", "MAY") are translated with the correct force in the target language.
The translator submits the completed .po file back to the pipeline. This may happen via: - Git commit + push - Weblate/Crowdin sync - File upload to the coordinator

The translator works through each msgid, producing msgstr translations. They: - Follow the domain glossary for technical terms - Preserve placeholder tokens ({1}, {2}) in position - Mark uncertain translations as #fuzzy - Note any source ambiguities for the coordinator

Record the translation's standing in translations/<locale>/status.json. The `official` input says which: `false` records it as unofficial ({ official: false, generatedBy, generatedAt }), usable but shown with a warning badge; `true` records the human sign-off with the SHA-256 of the source .md, so a later change to the source marks it stale.

terms.prefLabel: Record it in library/ as referenced
terms.definition: The referenced branch. Nothing is fetched and no bytes are written: the catalogue record says where the asset is and that we hold none. A reference is not a fetch — it stays navigable without being held, and materializing it later is `materialize-remote.bpmn`'s decision, with its purpose and five gates, not this flow's.

terms.prefLabel: Extract its metadata into the KG
terms.definition: THE METADATA STEP. What enters the knowledge graph is the asset's INDEX — what it is, how big, what type, when it says it was written — and, for a container, what is in it; its contents do not go in unless somebody asks, with a reason. The tool is `cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-assets.ts`, writing a `folio-extraction/v1` record (`schemas/content/extraction.ts`). The media type is sniffed from the leading bytes, never taken from the extension.

terms.prefLabel: Place it in uploads/ by a declared route
terms.definition: THE FIRST LINK: everything downstream of here takes a file that is already in the queue, so without this step how the file got there is governed by nothing. WHAT THIS STEP IS. The basic flow's ACCEPT step: choosing an arrival route, writing the bytes into the declared queue of the instance that will own them, and discharging what that route does not discharge for you. The routes, what each writer owes, and the two that are mechanisms against the one that is a persona are in the `upload-routes` skill; `upload-url` composes the forge URL for the web route from the declaration rather than from a literal, because a hand-written one can 404. WHY A PLAIN `bpmn:task` AND NOT A `userTask`. A `userTask` asserts a human performs it, and this lane is "Contributor (human or agent)" because both do; asserting human-only would be an `activity-fulfilment-kind` contradiction. A plain task asserts nothing about the performer. WHY THE BEAN OP IS `note` AND NOT `claim`. Placing a file claims nothing; it adds to a queue. What it owes the work plan is visibility. A note against the ingestion bean is what makes the queue's growth something another session can see.

The materialized branch. The asset lands in library/<slug>/ with its metadata record, its provenance and its fixity. The folder name IS the citation key, so a citation and a directory are the same string. The upload is then RETIRED, not left and not deleted: it moves to fsh-guts/uploads/ beside a sidecar naming where it came from and when, and `check:uploads-retired` finds one that was not. A refining process that derives content from the bytes does so before that retirement; `library-ingestion` carries the rule.

A step because sources do contradict themselves (one colour given two values on different pages). A contradiction silently resolved is indistinguishable from one nobody noticed, so it is kept as data and the reading taken is stated as a choice.

surface / ink / edge / accent, shared across every kind. A palette per kind would be three spellings of "accent colour", free to disagree about what an accent IS. Where the source is SILENT on a role, say so and mark the value a choice rather than dressing an invention as a measurement.

terms.prefLabel: Read the guide's own stated rules
terms.definition: From the INGESTED document's sections, not from a screenshot and not inferred from a site that happens to use the brand. Units stay as the source gives them: rewriting 29.7cm as millimetres is a conversion nobody asked for and a chance to be wrong.

Read the ROLE, never the prettiest value. Bootstrap's --blue is a scale entry and --primary is the role; DSpace sets them differently, and taking the brand-looking one is the hardcoding schemas/ui/theme.ts exists to end. Column widths come from declared columns, never from breakpoints: a breakpoint is a viewport.

THEME REVIEW HAPPENS HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE: graphical assets are reviewed at ingestion, in the context of the website or app design they are for. So this step CALLS `theme-ui-review.bpmn`. WHAT THE CALL COSTS, stated rather than hidden. The subprocess has a human step, `R_Judge`: a person looks at the ingested assets laid out in their design at a web and a mobile width. So ingesting a THEME SOURCE is attended at that step. Ingesting anything else stays unattended: it never reaches this subprocess. THE AUTOMATED CHECK IS INSIDE THE CALL. "A theme sets the stripe's hue; it never sets its width to zero" — colour alone carrying a whole signal fails WCAG SC 1.4.1, and the WHO guide agrees ("Never red with green, never blue with yellow"). That check is `A_Accessibility` in the called process, which measures contrast against the real ground and requires a non-colour channel wherever colour carries meaning.

terms.prefLabel: Check the .jsonld siblings are in sync
terms.definition: Run the five --check generators in one job — the JSON-LD context, block siblings, library nodes, site graph, then the label-resolution and emitter tests. Any committed .jsonld that differs from what its generator now produces fails the PR, because a stale generated file is still consulted.
A repository cut changes the substrate every other process binds to; that is a person's decision. Declining leaves the graph declared, detangled, isolated and split in place.

What the work is and why, what is already measured with its provenance, how it will be done, and what would falsify the approach. The work item is already taken up when the process starts, so a sibling session sees the work before the brief is written. Here the work is a separation: what is separating, and why.

The parent pins the pair (a commit while staging, a version once released) — a code dependency as a `source.remote` instance in its root `index.config.json` (remote-mount skill), never a submodule — repoints its imports, and keeps its own copy until it is green with the dependency declared.
The owner creates the content and tools repositories and their Pages. Nothing is committed to them before this.

The one commit worth reverting, made only after the parent consumes the release and every identifier dereferences. It retires the parent's copy, frozen, never refreshed and never rendered, rather than deleting it. Where the copy goes is the sub-kg-lifecycle skill's stage 13; this diagram does not name that store, because the published graph must not.

Run `bun run cat separation:cutover:check --site` in the SEPARATED repository (Tool `separation-cutover-check`). Six conditions, each decided by an existing gate and none assumed: every declared layer mounted at its pin; every path a declaration names resolves (`check:declaration-resolution` — directories, assets, visualisers, needs); no wiring still names the monorepo (`livesAt`, a submodule, a reusable workflow, a path into the old checkout); no import or reference against the layer order; and the site builds from the mounts alone. A finding inside a mounted layer is upstream's and is listed, not counted.

The owner decides from the measured signals, and also decides the address base for its identifiers, where verdicts about it live, and what its tools repository owns. Declining is a real outcome: the graph stays where it is.

The graph-detanglement practice, all of its gates: declared in place, zero wrong-direction edges on every axis, and standing alone with its own declaration, namespace and artefact. A plain task on purpose, not a call to graph-detanglement.bpmn: that process ends in its own authorise-and-extract steps, which here are stages 9-13 of this one, and calling it would run them twice.

terms.prefLabel: Drain: land, close or re-target the open PRs
terms.definition: Work the PRs `seed:ready` named until the source settles: land or close the heavy movers and the next layer's PRs, bring the layer's open PRs to five or fewer, and finish any move in flight. Fix a red rehearsal or a discovery miss where it is. Nothing is seeded from here; it goes back to the gateway, which re-asks.

terms.prefLabel: 5 · Move harness output about it to the host
terms.definition: QA verdicts, translation templates, the exported graph and the glossary ledger are harness output ABOUT the graph: they live with the harness (kgQaHomeFor, translationsHomeFor). The content keeps only what its own checks need; the leak test's pending list is empty. The one exception is a separated layer that declares a `qa` directory of its own with `storage`: its verdicts are its own repository's, published to that repository's qa-reports branch (step 10), and read by a host at the commit it pins.
The declaration carries name, version, iriBase, needs and nodeSchemas. A base move is `bun run iri:sync -- --from <old base>`, once; then `iri:sync:check` and `check:node-iris` are green.

Files and bytes per instance, clone cost (`bun run cat health`), gate time, merge contention, the candidate's cohesion and cut (`kg:detangle`), wrong-direction edges, and the would-be tools package's import cone. Recorded in the work context; none alone is a trigger.

Every identifier the content mints is a file some step publishes: /v<major>/, for what programs read and pages people read alike; the exact release is the pin's. Name collisions between published files are resolved here.

terms.prefLabel: Report what moves — sizes, what breaks
terms.definition: The agent reports and waits: what would move, how large, what in the parent breaks, and the rollback. `deletion-requires-confirmation` is not a courtesy to waive: an agent never removes or relocates a durable artefact on its own initiative.

Copy the content and the tools alone into a temporary directory, with nothing else on the path, and run the tools' checks there. An empty tree must exit non-zero, so a rehearsal over nothing cannot pass.
Tag each repository, publish /v<major>/. From here the two are versioned independently; a tools release lists the content majors it supports.

Seed main, then bring the content and the tools in as reviewed pull requests with their history, so neither repository's first commit is unreviewable. The seed includes every publisher the declaration promises (`sub-kg-lifecycle` stage 10): a `qa` directory with `storage` needs `.github/workflows/publish-qa.yml`, the caller of the tools layer's `layer-qa-publish.yml`, and `test/results/` ignored. Without it the declared store is never written, and once the layer stops committing its results no reader finds them.

Create <name>-tools as a sibling directory and move the code: the Zod source, the generators, the README and diagram writers, the content checks. Cut its import cone to its own files and declared packages. Both start at the content's version.
After the release is live, every published identifier resolves to the file it names.

terms.prefLabel: Publish to the origin (a cache may front it)
terms.definition: Reach host behaviour through publication.host, never by assuming GitHub Pages' behaviour — Pages CANNOT serve application/ld+json and a local server can. A CDN in front is a layer, not the host: the canonical URL stays the origin's, and the cache is an accelerated route to the same bytes. Uploading and exposing are separable steps on purpose, because collapsing them removes the last moment at which a bad URL layout can still be caught.

The serialization alone is not a package. A package is an addressable set — the JSON-LD, the assets it references, and a manifest naming every file with its digest and byte count. The manifest is what makes a REMOVED file detectable, which a per-file signature cannot do on its own.
Apply the editorial scope mechanically and report what it removed. A selection that reports nothing cannot be told from one that ran over an empty rule.

kg-export, already built and host-agnostic by design. Every edge term declared {"@type": "@id"} — without that coercion the document is a list of records that merely LOOKS linked, and the node IRIs are fragments of the document's own @id so the graph is mergeable with anyone else's.

Money, network traffic, graph size, latency. Each needs a NUMBER and each number needs a denominator, because a constraint with no denominator is a preference: "the graph is too big" is not a finding, "6.2 MB per publication against a 100 GB free tier" is. Say which figures were measured, which were quoted from a vendor, and which could not be obtained; a figure from a chat message is none of the three.

terms.prefLabel: Record the decision as still open
terms.definition: An undetermined decision is DATA, not silence. It is recorded with what it waits on and what would settle it, so the next session can tell "nobody has chosen" from "somebody chose and did not write it down" — the same third state bean-blocking keeps for a block with no expiry.

terms.prefLabel: Human eyes on the rendered artefact
terms.definition: Easy to drop because merging to main looks like an approval. It is not: merging approves the CHANGE, and this approves what a reader will actually see. A description cannot stand in for it (`continual-progress`).

terms.prefLabel: Decide what may leave the repository
terms.definition: EDITORIAL, and it is stage 1 rather than a filter bolted to the exporter. kg-export produces the WHOLE graph because inspection wants the whole graph; a portal wants what its readers may see. Running the second as the first is how a QA verdict, a bean's blocking note or an unpublished draft reaches a public cache. Decided once, here, rather than at each consumer.

terms.prefLabel: Verify what arrived against what was signed
terms.definition: Against a GDHCN DID trustlist, which means the verifier needs THE NETWORK and not only the bytes — the key is resolved from the trustlist rather than read out of the package. The trustlist is itself static JSON served from a CDN (`tng-cdn.who.int`), and its path is a hierarchical filter — domain, participant, key usage, with `-` as a wildcard — so a verifier fetches the slice it needs rather than the whole list. The stage that gets dropped, because every other stage produces something visible and this one produces nothing when it passes. A package that is signed and never verified is a package whose signature is decoration. A portal that CANNOT verify reports `unknown` — a portal nobody asked is not a portal that checked.

terms.prefLabel: Sign the package and/or each asset
terms.definition: THE TRUST ANCHOR IS GDHCN, SPECIFIED BY THE WHO SMART TRUST IG. READ OFF THAT IG rather than from general knowledge: a GDHCN trustlist distributes KEY MATERIAL as W3C DID documents, and says nothing about what you wrap your bytes in — the health-certificate envelope is a separate specification in the same IG, and a document package is not a health certificate. So what is settled is where a verifier GETS THE KEY, not what it verifies. A portal that can fetch the bytes but not reach the trustlist cannot verify, which is `unknown` and not a failure — air-gapped is a declared deployment value, so that case is answered rather than assumed away. Still OPEN and unread: the rotation and revocation model, and whether a document-package signature can be expressed for a GDHCN-aware verifier at all. Two schemes with different properties remain to choose between, and the trustlist does not choose between them. A PACKAGE signature over the manifest verifies the SET — nothing added, removed or altered — and must be reissued whenever any file changes. A PER-ASSET signature verifies one file independently, which is what an edge cache serving one asset can actually check, and it cannot detect a removal because there is nothing left to verify. They compose; composing them is the safer and more expensive default, and it is the deployment's choice rather than the pipeline's.

Restrictions, copyright, retention and source loss, each answered permitted, refused or unknown. They are four answers to one decision, and Gateway_Gates reads them with size through decisions/materialization-gate.dmn. RESTRICTIONS. 'No restrictions known in context' is a STATE, not a green light. GateVerdict is three-valued for this reason alone, and `unknown` is never rendered as `permitted`. COPYRIGHT. What the licence permits for THIS bitstream, and separately whether it permits the derivation. LICENSE-CONTENT.md exists in this repository and the ingestion pipeline does not read it. RETENTION. A copy with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one — the same argument bean-blocking makes about a block with no expiry. An ARCHIVAL copy is the exception and it is a specification rather than an omission: freshness() reports it `permanent`, not `no-expiry`. SOURCE LOSS. Not hypothetical. The one IRIS record this repository holds carries a handle on iris.wpro.who.int, a regional instance merged into the global one. Only an ARCHIVAL copy of the original bytes discharges this; a working copy cannot, because the derived sections are not the publication.

The node's state moves from `referenced` to `materialized`, carrying purpose, localPath, gates and (archival) fixity. There is NO default state: a node that has not said is invalid, because 'the author did not say' and 'the author said they could not tell' are different facts.

Resolve the request against the source's descriptor (one per corpus, in the declared sources/ of the instance that owns it, e.g. who-iris/sources/), read against cat-harness/schemas/library/source-descriptor.ts BEFORE any gate. Three things come from it and none may be guessed. (1) Which subset strategies the source supports — supportsSubset(). (2) Whether a subset stands on its own: when subsetIsSelfContained is false (mathlib), the request is closed over its dependencies here, and every gate after this one is asked about the CLOSURE, because a subset that omits what its members depend on is not a smaller corpus, it is one that does not build.
